definition: Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) is a federal statute addressing copyright issues arising from digital technology and the internet. It was enacted as Public Law 105-304 and signed into law on October 28, 1998, by President Bill Clinton. The statute implemented the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) Copyright Treaty of 1996 into U.S. law, combined several additional proposed bills, and filled gaps in domestic copyright protections. The DMCA strengthened copyright law in several areas. It expanded protections against new methods of digital infringement and established mechanisms for digital rights management (technological measures to control access and use). It also introduced safe harbor provisions that shield internet service providers from monetary liability for user infringement if they comply with specific requirements. Under 17 U.S.C. § 512, to enjoy this liability protection, the internet service providers must not have actual knowledge of infringement or be aware of circumstances from which infringement is apparent, not receive financial benefit directly from the infringing activity, and respond expeditiously to remove or address the infringing material. The anti-circumvention provisions, under 17 U.S.C. § 1201, protect a copyright owner from circumvention (i.e., bypassing, removing, deactivating, or impairing) of technological measures dictum / Digital Millennium Copyright Act Dictionary compilation | 26 September 2026 that control access to a copyrighted work. In Universal City Studios, Inc. v. Corley, 273 F.3d 429 (2001), the defendants challenged the DMCA under the First Amendment and fair use exemption. The defendants lost at trial, and the Second Circuit affirmed the decision.
